metaDescription: Grab trending AI prompts for photo edits, paste them into Gemini or ChatGPT, drop in your selfie, and get figurine, retro saree, and 90s film looks in minutes.
bodyHtml:
AI prompts are the fastest way to get those trending photo edits you keep scrolling past, the tiny figurine of yourself, the retro saree portrait, the grainy 90s film look, and the grid above is full of ones you can copy and run in a minute. Most of them are tuned for Google's Gemini image model, the one people online keep calling nano banana, but they also work in ChatGPT, Midjourney, and DALL-E. The idea is simple. You paste a prompt, add your own photo or your own idea, and the tool builds the picture. No editing software, no design background, nothing to install on a laptop. A lot of people doing this are on their phone, trying a trend they saw in a reel an hour ago.

What trending AI prompts really are

A trending prompt is just a written recipe that lots of people are using right now to get the same look. Someone makes a striking edit, posts it, and the wording behind it spreads. Within a week half your feed has the same style. That is why a tag or a search term can feel mysterious. The picture went viral but the actual prompt got cut off, so you end up hunting for the words. The good news is you do not need the exact original. The tools respond to what you describe, not to a secret phrase. A clear prompt that names the look, the mood, and a few details will get you very close.

Trends also move fast. What was everywhere last month can feel tired now, and a new look takes over. So treat any prompt as a starting point you adjust, not a fixed formula. Copy one that is close, run it, then change a word or two and run again.

The looks people make with AI prompts right now

If you want to ride a trend, it helps to know which ones are doing the rounds. These are the styles that keep showing up in nano banana and ChatGPT edits, and the grid above has prompts for most of them.

  • The 3D figurine. You as a small collectible toy standing in a clear box on a desk, sometimes with a tiny stand and a printed label. This one blew up because it keeps your face but turns you into a product shot.
  • Retro saree or vintage Bollywood portrait. Warm film grain, soft studio light, an old-poster feel. Hugely popular for solo and couple photos.
  • The 90s polaroid look. Slight blur, flash glare, that washed colour you get from a disposable camera. People love it for a candid, nostalgic feel.
  • Miniature or tiny world. You shrunk down inside an everyday object, a coffee cup, a bookshelf, a plant pot.
  • Couple and pre-wedding shots. Two uploaded faces placed into a cinematic scene, a rainy street, a field at golden hour.
  • The clean headshot. A plain selfie turned into a tidy professional photo for a profile picture, with a neutral background and even light.

Match AI prompts to the look you want

The fastest way to get a result you like is to name the look and then add the two or three details that make it specific. This table pairs common trends with the mood they give and the words worth adding to the prompt.

Look you wantThe feel it givesWhat to add to the prompt
3D figurine in a boxPlayful, collectible, product shot'clear plastic box, small stand, soft studio light, keep my face exact'
Retro saree portraitWarm, nostalgic, cinematic'film grain, warm tones, soft side light, vintage studio backdrop'
90s film polaroidCandid, washed, real'disposable camera, flash, slight blur, faded colour, date stamp'
Tiny miniature worldCute, surreal, fun'shrunk down, sitting inside a coffee cup, shallow depth of field'
Professional headshotClean, neutral, sharp'plain grey background, even lighting, natural skin, sharp focus'

How to write or tweak AI prompts so they actually work

The order inside a prompt matters more than people think. I usually go subject first, then style, then the small stuff. So it reads like: who is in the shot, what style it should be in, then lighting, background, and aspect ratio. If you are editing your own photo, say plainly that you want the face kept the same, because that is the part most edits get wrong.

  1. Name the subject. 'A photo of me' or 'this couple' if you uploaded faces.
  2. Name the style. Figurine, retro saree, 90s film, miniature, headshot.
  3. Add mood and light. Warm, soft, dramatic, golden hour, studio.
  4. Set the frame. Portrait, square, or wide, and where you plan to post it.
  5. Lock the face. For edits, add something like 'keep my face and features unchanged'.

Then change one thing at a time. If you swap the background, the lighting, and the outfit all at once and the result is worse, you will not know which change broke it. Small steps win here.

Tip: save one prompt that gives you a result you like, keep it in your notes, and reuse it as a base. Editing the changing parts is far quicker than writing a fresh prompt every time.

Where to run AI prompts: Gemini, ChatGPT, or Midjourney

For trending photo edits where you upload your own face, Gemini's image model, the nano banana one, is the one most people reach for. It holds a likeness well, it is quick, and it is free to try in the Gemini app, with API use costing only a few cents per image. ChatGPT is the easy starting point if you already have it open, and it handles photo edits and generation in the same chat. Midjourney makes gorgeous images from scratch and is strong on artistic styles, but it is built more for generating new scenes than for editing a selfie you upload. If your goal is a trend that starts with your own photo, start with Gemini or ChatGPT. If you want pure art from a written idea, Midjourney is worth the time.

Common AI prompts mistakes and quick fixes

Most disappointing results come down to a handful of repeat problems.

  • The face changes. Add an explicit line telling the tool to keep your features, and upload a clear, well-lit photo so it has something solid to copy.
  • The prompt is too long. A wall of adjectives confuses the model. Trim it to the parts you actually care about.
  • You asked for too much at once. Three new looks in one prompt usually muddles all three. Pick one trend per try.
  • Wrong shape. If the crop is off, state the aspect ratio you want and where it is going, like a profile picture or a story.
  • Text comes out garbled. Image models still struggle with words inside a picture, so keep any on-image text short or skip it.

A quick routine for using AI prompts fast

When I want something usable in a couple of minutes, I run the same loop.

  1. Pick a prompt from the grid above that matches the trend I want.
  2. Paste it into Gemini or ChatGPT and attach my own photo if it is an edit.
  3. Add my two or three specifics, the background, the light, the mood.
  4. Run it, look at what worked, change one word, and run again.
  5. Keep the version that looks right and save the prompt for next time.

That loop is the whole thing. Trends will keep shifting, and the figurine look or the retro portrait will eventually give way to something new. The skill that lasts is knowing how to grab a close prompt, point it at your own photo, and nudge it until it lands. Start with one from the grid above and run it twice before you judge it.

faqs.q: What is the nano banana prompt everyone is using?
faqs.a: Nano banana is the nickname for Google's Gemini image model, used for photo edits like figurines, retro portraits, and couple shots. There is no single magic prompt. People share wording that names a look, then add their own photo. Copy a prompt from the grid above, paste it into the Gemini app, attach your selfie, and adjust.

faqs.q: How do I make the 3D figurine photo of myself?
faqs.a: Upload a clear photo of yourself, then use a prompt that asks for a small collectible figurine of you inside a clear plastic box, with a stand and soft studio light. Add a line telling the tool to keep your face exact. Run it, then tweak the box or label wording until it looks right.

faqs.q: Which app is best for trending AI photo prompts?
faqs.a: For edits that start with your own face, the Gemini app and its nano banana model hold a likeness well and are free to try. ChatGPT works too and is easy if you already have it open. Midjourney is better for making art from scratch than for editing a selfie you upload.

faqs.q: Why does the AI change my face in the edit?
faqs.a: Most models drift unless you tell them not to. Add a clear instruction like keep my face and features unchanged, and upload a sharp, well-lit photo so the tool has a solid reference. If it still changes, simplify the rest of the prompt so the face is the main thing it focuses on.

faqs.q: Do these prompts cost money to use?
faqs.a: Trying them is usually free. The Gemini app lets you test image edits at no cost, and ChatGPT includes some image use on its plans. Heavy use through an API runs only a few cents per image. For casual trend photos on your phone, you can get results without paying anything.
